content: Cytomegalovirus infection that occurs after the age of one month and affects organs other than the liver, spleen, or lymph nodes is a significant clinical concern. Disseminated mycobacterial disease, excluding tuberculosis, is another critical condition. Candida infections involving the trachea, bronchi, or lungs are also notable. Acquired HIV-related rectovesical fistulas, cerebral or B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and HIV encephalopathy are severe complications associated with HIV. Tuberculosis (TB) can occur at any CD4 count, and the percentage of CD4 cells should be considered when available. For children under 18 months of age who are seropositive, a presumptive diagnosis of stage 4 HIV disease requires confirmation through virological testing or an HIV antibody test after 18 months of age. All infants diagnosed with HIV under 60 months of age should immediately begin antiretroviral therapy (ART), regardless of their clinical or immunological status. While ART cannot cure HIV, it significantly reduces mortality and morbidity and improves the quality of life for children. The standard first-line treatment involves a combination of three antiretroviral drugs to suppress viral replication and halt disease progression. Fixed-dose combinations are preferred over syrups or single drugs as they improve adherence and reduce costs. Clinicians must be familiar with national pediatric HIV treatment guidelines, as the principles of ART and first-line drug choices for children are similar to those for adults. However, suitable formulations for children may not always be available, particularly for protease inhibitors. Children metabolize protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) faster than adults, necessitating higher equivalent doses to achieve therapeutic drug levels. Drug dosages must be adjusted as the child grows to prevent under-dosing and the development of resistance. Dosages are calculated based on body weight or surface area, with weight bands simplifying pediatric dosing regimens. ART for children includes three main classes of drugs: nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), NNRTIs, and protease inhibitors. First-line regimens for children under three years of age typically include lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) plus two NRTIs, regardless of prior exposure to nevirapine (NVP). For children aged three years and older, efavirenz (EFV) is the preferred NNRTI, especially for once-daily therapy, although NVP may be used as an alternative. EFV is also the NNRTI of choice for children on rifampicin if ART must begin before completing anti-TB therapy. Side effects of ART should be monitored regularly. Common side effects include headache, abdominal pain, anemia, hypersensitivity reactions, and gastrointestinal symptoms, depending on the specific drug. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) may occur after initiating ART, particularly in children with very low CD4 levels. IRIS often involves the unmasking or reactivation of latent infections, such as TB, pneumocystis pneumonia, or herpes simplex virus. Most cases resolve spontaneously or with anti-inflammatory treatment, but severe cases may require corticosteroids or temporary ART discontinuation. Vaccination is essential for HIV-exposed and infected children. They should receive all vaccines in the Expanded Programme for Immunization, including Haemophilus influenzae type B and pneumococcal vaccines, unless severely immunocompromised. BCG vaccination should not be given to children known to be HIV-infected due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease. Yellow fever vaccine is contraindicated in children with symptomatic HIV infection. ART failure may result from poor adherence, inadequate drug levels, prior drug resistance, or insufficient drug potency. Treatment failure is identified through clinical, immunological, or virological criteria. When confirmed, the entire regimen should be switched to a second-line combination, including at least three new drugs, one or more from a new class. Boosted protease inhibitors, such as LPV/r, are recommended for second-line regimens after failure of an NNRTI-based first-line regimen.
